analysis.one_liner: Taxes 95% of large corporations' profits above their pre-pandemic levels.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have taxed away 95% of large corporations' profits above their 2015–2019 inflation-adjusted levels, died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a temporary "excess profits" tax through 2024: corporations with at least $500 million in average annual sales would pay a 95% tax on profits above their inflation-adjusted 2015–2019 average, on top of normal taxes. It was aimed at companies posting record profits while consumer prices rose sharply in 2021–2022. It never got a hearing, a vote, or support beyond its two Senate sponsors.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the federal Treasury would have collected the tax revenue (the bill does not say how it would be spent), and consumers facing 2021–2022 price increases could have benefited if the tax discouraged companies from pushing prices and margins far above pre-pandemic norms. Corporations would still keep 25% of profits above the baseline, and profits up to the baseline entirely.

how_it_helps.text: It would impose a 95% tax on the portion of profits exceeding a company's own inflation-adjusted 2015–2019 average, targeting the windfall many large corporations reported while prices rose for consumers.
It applies only to corporations with average annual gross receipts of at least $500 million over three years, so small businesses are untouched.

It includes guardrails critics of windfall taxes usually demand: the tax is capped at 75% of a company's modified taxable income so it cannot push a firm into a net loss, and it sunsets after tax year 2024.
It broadens the executive pay deduction limit (Section 162(m)) so companies cannot avoid the cap by classifying more people as non-employees.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations (excluding real estate investment trusts, regulated investment companies, and S corporations) with average annual gross receipts of at least $500 million would pay the tax, at 95% of profits above their inflation-adjusted pre-pandemic baseline, up to 75% of modified taxable income. To the extent such companies pass taxes on through prices or reduced investment, some cost could fall on consumers and workers.

drawbacks.text: The baseline is arbitrary: a 95% rate hits any large company that legitimately grew or became more profitable after 2015–2019, not only those profiting from the inflation spike, which can discourage expansion and investment by exactly the firms doing well.

Economists across the spectrum generally agree that some share of corporate taxes is passed on to consumers in higher prices or to workers in lower wages, so part of the burden might land on the people the bill is meant to help.
The bill was introduced with no plan for spending the revenue and no hearing to test the design; it expired after tax year 2024, making it a one-off levy rather than a durable rule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax is bluntly designed: a 95% rate on any profit growth above a 2015–2019 baseline will hit companies whose gains reflect genuine growth, not just inflation-driven windfalls, and some burden would likely reach consumers and workers. The 75%-of-income cap and 2024 sunset soften the worst outcomes, and the revenue would have been substantial. On balance it was a targeted response to record corporate margins during a price spike, but a rough one that never received a hearing where its design flaws could be weighed and fixed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died when that Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Sanders introduced the bill on March 28, 2022, with Sen. Markey as its sole cosponsor, during a period of high inflation and record corporate profit margins.

It was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day of introduction; the full action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote at any point afterward.
Only one of 48 Senate Democrats signed on beyond the independent sponsor, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2023, with the bill still parked in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations with post-pandemic profits above pre-pandemic levels kept 100% of those profits untaxed, and no senator was ever forced to cast a public vote on the tax.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large corporations, whose excess profits went untaxed

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ending Corporate Greed Act on March 28, 2022 and referred it to the Finance Committee.

for.name: Ed Markey
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill's action history ends at the referral.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever took place; only one of 48 Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill, so partisan lines were never formally tested, though the lack of Democratic cosponsors signaled the party would not take it up.

industries.industry: Large corporations (esp. oil, pharmaceutical, food, and shipping companies reporting record margins)
industries.note: The bill would have taxed 95% of their profits above inflation-adjusted 2015–2019 levels, through 2024. Its death meant those companies kept all pandemic-era excess profits; the industry had nothing on the record against it because the bill never advanced that far.

The bill would have extended the deduction limit on executive pay (Section 162(m)) to all individuals serving a company, not just named top officers, reducing the tax benefit of large pay packages. The provision died with the bill.
